paragraphs: This paper asks whether one pretrained model can forecast many kinds of time series without being trained again for each new dataset. The motivation comes from language models: broad pretraining might produce reusable predictive capabilities. Here, the desired capability is estimating future values from past observations across different forecasting settings.

The authors build a decoder-style attention model that processes the input using patches. They pretrain it on a large collection containing both real-world and synthetic time series. This combines a forecasting architecture with varied training data, aiming to make the resulting model useful immediately on previously unseen datasets.

Experiments suggest that this approach can produce accurate zero-shot forecasts across different domains, prediction horizons, and temporal granularities. On a variety of public datasets, its accuracy approaches that of leading supervised models trained for each dataset individually. The finding supports the possibility of broadly reusable forecasting models; it does not establish that a single pretrained model always matches a specialized one.
icml-2024-a-decoder-only-foundation-mode.tldr: A pretrained decoder-style model produces zero-shot time-series forecasts approaching specialized supervised models on varied public datasets.

paragraphs: Active clustering uses strategically chosen human judgments about pairs of examples to improve how data are grouped. The challenge is making those judgments count: conventional methods can require too many queries when datasets are large and contain many classes. This paper develops A3S to improve clustering while reducing that annotation burden.

A3S begins with an initial grouping produced by an adaptive clustering algorithm. It then adjusts that grouping through aggregation and splitting, using pairwise constraints to guide the changes. Its adjustment strategy draws on an information-theoretic analysis of gains in normalized mutual information, connecting the choice of changes to a quantitative measure of clustering quality.

The authors provide a provable improvement result for their cluster adjustment and report extensive experiments on diverse real-world datasets. In those evaluations, A3S reaches desired clustering results using substantially fewer human queries than existing methods. The contribution is therefore both a quality-driven way to refine clusters and evidence that this refinement can make active clustering more scalable.
icml-2024-a3s-a-general-active-clusterin.tldr: A3S strategically merges and splits initial clusters, improving clustering quality while requiring fewer human pairwise judgments in experiments.

paragraphs: Finding repeating patterns in noisy time series matters for applications such as health monitoring and behavior analysis. Many learning methods depend on labels or clean reference signals. Self-supervised alternatives can require carefully designed signal transformations, and overly strong transformations can make the learned representations collapse to the same point.

The proposed method detects periodicity without labels and without tailored mechanisms for generating positive or negative examples. Its central idea is to retain information from the original samples in the learned representations. This addresses collapse without imposing constraints on the variance of representations across a batch, changing how the method preserves useful differences between signals.

The authors evaluate the approach on three time-series tasks against leading learning methods. They report consistent improvements over prior work, with performance improvements described as exceeding 45–50%. These findings support the usefulness of the approach in the tested settings. The broader contribution is a way to learn periodic structure while reducing dependence on supervision and task-specific example construction.
icml-2024-an-unsupervised-approach-for-p.tldr: An unsupervised method detects periodic signals by preserving sample information, avoiding labels and tailored positive or negative example generation.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate the average difference between two treatments using as few samples as possible. The target is a confidence interval with a specified maximum width and a specified maximum probability of missing the true effect. Treatment assignments can adapt as observations accumulate, making allocation part of the estimation problem.

The authors first derive a lower bound on the expected sample size needed by any qualifying adaptive policy. For small error probabilities, that bound involves a non-convex optimization problem. They construct a plug-in policy that asymptotically matches it. When both the interval width and error probability are small, the optimal allocation proportions follow the treatments' outcome standard deviations.

Because the first policy can be computationally expensive, the authors develop an alternative informed by the lower-bound analysis. It remains asymptotically optimal when both requirements become stringent while being computationally efficient. Numerical comparisons show similar performance between the policies at practical parameter values, connecting the theoretical allocation result to a more tractable procedure.
icml-2024-asymptotically-optimal-and-com.tldr: Adaptive A/B testing policies achieve asymptotically optimal sample use for treatment-effect confidence intervals, including a computationally efficient alternative.

paragraphs: Offline optimization searches for promising designs using an existing dataset, often because new physical experiments are expensive. A learned surrogate predicts the value of candidate designs and guides the search. The difficulty is that optimization can move beyond the region covered by the data, where those predictions may become unreliable.

This paper focuses on sensitivity to small changes in the surrogate's parameters. The authors connect a narrow prediction margin with this sensitivity and ask whether making the surrogate less sensitive can improve optimization. They develop a sensitivity measure that can itself be optimized, then use it to construct a regularizer for guiding surrogate learning.

The regularizer can be applied to a wide range of offline optimizers, making it a component that can complement existing approaches. Extensive benchmark experiments demonstrate that the sensitivity-based development works synergistically with prior methods. Its significance is to make surrogate sensitivity an explicit optimization concern, alongside the broader problem of finding high-value candidates from a fixed body of observations.
icml-2024-boosting-offline-optimizers-wi.tldr: A sensitivity-based regularizer improves offline optimization by helping control how surrogate predictions respond to parameter perturbations.

paragraphs: Collaborative learning seeks accurate classifiers for several data distributions while minimizing the total number of samples collected. A common assumption is that one classifier can work well for every distribution. This paper relaxes that requirement, allowing the distributions to have different labeling functions while retaining a weaker realizability assumption.

Under that weaker assumption, the authors show that learning can still be sample-efficient. Their algorithm minimizes empirical prediction error over an augmented hypothesis class. They analyze the complexity of this expanded class through its VC dimension, using that bound to establish how much data the learning procedure requires.

The computational picture is less favorable in general: empirical risk minimization over the augmented class is NP-hard. This supplies evidence against broadly efficient computation, rather than proving that every possible learner must be inefficient. For two special cases, however, the authors provide learners that are efficient in both samples and computation. The paper thus separates the possibility of learning with limited data from the difficulty of carrying out that learning.
icml-2024-collaborative-learning-with-di.tldr: Collaborative learning remains sample-efficient under a weaker shared-structure assumption, although general computation is difficult and efficient learners are given for two special cases.

paragraphs: Training a diffusion model from corrupted examples raises a basic question: can it recover the underlying clean distribution? Existing ambient diffusion and SURE-based approaches use approximations that can hurt performance. This paper presents a framework with a proof that sampling from the uncorrupted distribution is possible using only noisy training data.

The technical construction applies Tweedie's formula twice and adds a consistency loss. Together, these allow sampling to extend to noise levels below the noise present in the observations. This matters because learning only at the observed noise level would leave a gap between the available training examples and the clean distribution the model is intended to generate.

The paper also presents evidence of memorization by identifying heavily corrupted training images that diffusion models reconstruct almost perfectly. In experiments fine-tuning Stable Diffusion XL with noisy examples, the proposed framework reduces memorization of the fine-tuning dataset while maintaining competitive performance. This supports corrupted-data training as a mitigation for memorization, without implying that it eliminates privacy or copyright concerns.
icml-2024-consistent-diffusion-meets-twe.tldr: A consistency-based diffusion framework provably recovers clean distributions from noisy training data and empirically reduces fine-tuning memorization.

paragraphs: Running neural networks on cryptographically protected data is computationally expensive, particularly when evaluating nonlinear activations. One speedup replaces a selected portion of those activations with linear operations. Such changes can greatly reduce runtime while barely affecting overall accuracy, making them attractive for privacy-preserving inference.

This paper shows that aggregate accuracy can conceal uneven consequences. Reducing the number of ReLU activations disproportionately lowers accuracy for minority groups compared with majority groups. The authors observe this problem across widely used datasets and architectures, indicating that the fairness cost is relevant across multiple evaluated settings.

To help explain the effect, the paper gives a mathematical interpretation under restricted assumptions about the decision boundary. Those assumptions delimit the theoretical explanation. The authors also show that a simple change to the fine-tuning procedure can mitigate the disparity. The practical implication is that evaluating this computational shortcut requires attention to group-level accuracy, and that the fine-tuning stage offers a way to address the observed imbalance.
icml-2024-disparate-impact-on-group-accu.tldr: Linearizing neural networks for faster private inference can disproportionately harm minority-group accuracy, with modified fine-tuning providing a mitigation.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how the brain's relatively static wiring supports changing patterns of neural activity. Its starting point is that connections between distant regions give the brain a geometry that may help explain those fluctuations. The authors develop a physics-informed deep model to study the relationship between anatomical structure and dynamic function.

The model represents evolving functional activity on a Riemannian manifold and learns mappings that describe its underlying features. Those mappings are constrained by graph-harmonic scattering transforms, which incorporate brain-wide connection geometry. This produces an architecture resembling an MLP-Mixer adapted to manifold-based representations, tying the learned transformations to the structure of the brain's network.

As a proof of concept, the approach offers a neural-manifold perspective on structure–function coupling. The authors propose that brain-wide oscillatory waves on connectome geometry excite neural activity, challenging an account confined to focal regions. This is a proposed interpretation developed through the model, rather than an established universal explanation of cognition or behavior.
icml-2024-exploring-the-enigma-of-neural.tldr: A geometry-constrained neural model explores how brain-wide connectivity and oscillatory waves may link anatomical structure to changing neural activity.

paragraphs: Neural networks can perform image super-resolution effectively, but explaining how they transform an image remains difficult. This paper approaches that question using signal processing. The authors begin with an observed response to an impulse input, which they call the sinc phenomenon, and use it as a starting point for analyzing network behavior.

Their method, Hybrid Response Analysis, separates the network into parallel linear and nonlinear systems. The analysis shows that the linear component acts as a low-pass filter, while the nonlinear component adds high-frequency information. This gives a more concrete account of the roles played by different parts of the transformation when producing a higher-resolution image.

The paper also introduces Frequency Spectrum Distribution Similarity, a metric for comparing how different frequency components are distributed in image-to-image tasks. It is intended to quantify the injected high-frequency information and capture nuances that traditional metrics may miss. Together, the decomposition and metric provide tools for interpreting super-resolution through the frequency content of its outputs.
icml-2024-exploring-the-low-pass-filteri.tldr: Hybrid Response Analysis interprets super-resolution networks as a linear low-pass component alongside a nonlinear component that adds high-frequency information.

paragraphs: Active exploration uses reinforcement learning to help choose experiments in a dynamical system. For finite Markovian systems, experiment design can be relaxed into Convex RL, which allows a broader notion of reward. The difficulty is scale: scientific experiment spaces can be so large that the existing framework becomes impractical.

The authors exploit known geometric structure in these spaces, such as permutation invariance in molecular design. They connect active exploration with MDP homomorphisms, a formal way to construct abstractions that use such structure. Their first contribution extends this formalism to Convex RL; their second analyzes how abstraction benefits sample efficiency.

These developments lead to the Geometric Active Exploration algorithm, which the authors study theoretically and experimentally in environments motivated by scientific discovery. The contribution is a formal connection between structural abstraction and the amount of experience needed for exploration. It shows how known geometry can become part of experimental planning, rather than leaving the agent to confront the full state space without that structure.
icml-2024-geometric-active-exploration-i.tldr: Geometric Active Exploration uses known state-space structure to build abstractions and formally analyze their benefits for sample-efficient experiment design.

paragraphs: Standard reinforcement learning commonly adds up rewards associated with visited states. That formulation can miss interactions: visiting two states together may be redundant or especially valuable. This paper introduces Global RL, where rewards are defined over complete trajectories so that the objective can account for relationships among the states an agent visits.

The framework represents negative interactions through submodularity, positive interactions through supermodularity, and mixed interactions through combinations of the two. These distinctions let the reward express effects that an additive objective overlooks. The authors then draw on submodular optimization to turn a Global RL problem into a sequence of conventional reinforcement-learning problems.

The resulting algorithmic scheme has approximation guarantees that depend on curvature, so the guarantee varies with the objective's structure. The paper also establishes hardness-of-approximation results and reports effective performance on several Global RL instances. Its contribution is both an expanded reward formulation and a way to approach it through familiar RL subproblems, while recognizing that these broader objectives have computational limits.
icml-2024-global-reinforcement-learning-.tldr: Global RL models interactions across trajectories and solves the resulting objectives through sequences of standard RL problems with curvature-dependent approximation guarantees.

paragraphs: Updating factual knowledge in a large language model can require expensive retraining or fine-tuning. Larimar approaches this problem by adding a distributed episodic memory to the model. This brain-inspired architecture gives the system a mechanism for dynamic, one-shot knowledge updates, making memory modification central to the editing process.

Across multiple fact-editing benchmarks, Larimar achieves accuracy comparable to highly competitive baselines, including when edits arrive sequentially. The authors report speedups of eight to ten times, depending on the underlying language model. They also describe the architecture as simple and independent of a particular base LLM, supporting its use across different models.

The paper extends memory control beyond adding or changing facts. It introduces mechanisms for selectively forgetting facts, preventing information leakage, and generalizing input context length, and demonstrates their effectiveness. These results position episodic memory as a way to manage several aspects of model knowledge. The empirical accuracy and speed findings concern the evaluated editing settings, with the reported speed advantage varying by base model.
icml-2024-larimar-large-language-models-.tldr: Larimar adds editable episodic memory to language models, enabling one-shot knowledge updates with competitive accuracy and reported eight-to-tenfold speedups.

paragraphs: In a partially observed environment, different places can produce indistinguishable observations, making navigation difficult. Predicting the next observation does not by itself provide an explicit map that a planner can query. This paper adds discrete bottlenecks to a transformer to learn compressed representations of an agent's observation and action history.

The transformer is trained to predict future observations. The authors then extract interpretable cognitive maps from the active bottleneck indices and pair those maps with an external solver for constrained path planning. This connects sequence prediction to planning through an explicit intermediate representation that describes the environment.

In the studied environments, the model preserves near-perfect predictive performance while solving shortest-path problems exponentially faster. It also produces interpretable representations from text and achieves higher in-context accuracy than vanilla sequence models. In new partially observed environments, the authors report near-perfect in-context prediction, accurate cognitive maps, and successful in-context path planning. The results support discrete bottlenecks as a route from predictive representations to usable environment maps.
icml-2024-learning-cognitive-maps-from-t.tldr: A transformer with discrete bottlenecks learns interpretable environment maps that support efficient planning through an external solver.

paragraphs: A single predictor may need to perform well for several subgroups, including groups that overlap. Multi-group learning formalizes that requirement instead of assessing the predictor only across the population as a whole. This paper studies the case where the groups have a hierarchical structure, making the relationships among groups part of the learning setting.

The authors design an algorithm that produces a deterministic decision tree predictor. The tree is interpretable, so the learned prediction rule has an explicit structure that can be examined. They establish near-optimal sample complexity, meaning the algorithm's data requirements are close to the best achievable for the setting addressed by their analysis.

The paper also evaluates the algorithm on real datasets with hierarchical groups and reports attractive generalization properties. The theoretical and empirical contributions address complementary questions: how efficiently the predictor can be learned, and how it behaves on real data. Together, they support hierarchical group structure as a useful basis for learning one interpretable predictor with multiple subgroup requirements.
icml-2024-multi-group-learning-for-hiera.tldr: An algorithm for hierarchical multi-group learning produces interpretable decision trees with near-optimal sample complexity and promising empirical generalization.

paragraphs: Community detection often assigns every node in a network to a cluster. This paper questions that assumption when meaningful communities exist only among some nodes. The remaining nodes may be scattered with respect to the community structure of interest, so forcing them into groups can distort the result.

The authors illustrate this issue with protein networks: some proteins belong to specific functional modules, while others participate in general processes or connect different modules. Their tight community detection method aims to identify the nodes that form meaningful communities while excluding scattered nodes. Deciding which nodes belong in the clustering is therefore part of the task.

The algorithm comes with a strong theoretical guarantee for identifying tight nodes and is designed to scale to large networks. Synthetic and real-data experiments demonstrate advantages over the alternatives studied. The contribution is a community-detection formulation that allows selective membership, helping preserve the interpretation of the communities when a full partition would introduce unwanted assignments.
icml-2024-network-tight-community-detect.tldr: Tight community detection identifies meaningful network communities while excluding scattered nodes that would distort a forced full partition.

paragraphs: Neural collapse describes a structured pattern in the final features of a classifier late in training. Features from the same class converge toward their class mean, and in the balanced setting the means form a symmetric geometric arrangement. This paper investigates how that picture changes when classes have different numbers of training examples.

The analysis uses cross-entropy loss under an unconstrained ReLU features model. Within this setting, examples within each class still collapse to a common representation. However, the class means converge to orthogonal vectors whose lengths depend on class sample counts, replacing the balanced characterization with geometry that reflects the imbalance.

The classifier weights also follow a structured relationship: they align with scaled and centered class means, with scaling determined by each class's sample count. The authors validate the results empirically using practical architectures and data. The contribution clarifies which parts of neural collapse persist under imbalance and how both feature geometry and classifier alignment change, with the theoretical conclusions tied to the stated model.
icml-2024-neural-collapse-for-cross-entr.tldr: Under an unconstrained ReLU features model, class imbalance preserves within-class collapse while changing class-mean geometry and classifier alignment according to class counts.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering methods are widely used, but their popularity exceeds the available theoretical understanding of the quality of their outputs. This paper studies cluster cohesion, focusing on bounds for the maximum cluster diameter produced by complete-link clustering in metric spaces. Diameter captures how far apart members of a cluster can be.

The authors improve existing bounds and obtain one that separates complete-link from single-link in terms of diameter approximation. This gives theoretical support to the common view that complete-link is better suited to producing compact clusters. The result concerns the stated compactness objective, rather than establishing that complete-link is preferable for every purpose.

The analysis also extends beyond complete-link. The authors show that their techniques yield upper bounds on cohesion for a broader class of linkage methods that includes average-link. The significance is a stronger mathematical account of familiar algorithms: it both distinguishes methods under a concrete quality criterion and supplies techniques for studying the cohesion of additional linkage rules.
icml-2024-new-bounds-on-the-cohesion-of-.tldr: Improved cohesion bounds distinguish complete-link from single-link for diameter approximation and extend to linkage methods including average-link.

paragraphs: Lagrangian relaxation handles difficult constraints in mixed-integer linear programs using multipliers that determine a bound on the optimal objective value. Finding strong multipliers usually involves iterative optimization, whose cost grows with the number of relaxed constraints. This paper learns to predict useful multipliers, distributing the effort of optimization across instances through training.

A graph neural network encoder receives a problem instance and its continuous-relaxation solution. It creates representations of the relaxed constraints, which a decoder converts into multipliers. Both components are trained directly against the quality of the resulting bound. The stated applicability covers compact MILP formulations with a Lagrangian relaxation that gives a tighter bound than continuous relaxation.

Experiments on Multi-Commodity Network Design and Generalized Assignment show that predicted multipliers close up to 85% of the gap between continuous relaxation and the best Lagrangian bound. They also provide strong starting points for iterative Lagrangian methods. Thus, the learned predictions can produce useful bounds directly and improve initialization when further optimization is desired.
icml-2024-predicting-lagrangian-multipli.tldr: A graph-based encoder–decoder predicts Lagrangian multipliers that produce strong MILP bounds and useful warm starts for iterative optimization.

paragraphs: An effect measured in a randomized trial may differ from the effect in a target population when characteristics that modify treatment effects have different distributions. Generalizing trial results is particularly difficult when the target population has covariate data but no observed outcomes. Limited trial sizes make estimating the complex supporting functions statistically infeasible in the problem studied.

The authors develop algorithms that supplement trial data with a prediction model trained on an additional observational study. Their approach does not require assumptions about that observational study. This allows the extra data to contribute predictions without requiring the observational source itself to satisfy conditions that would justify treating its associations as causal effects.

Theoretical and empirical results show improved generalization when the observational study is high-quality and robustness when it is not, including when it contains unmeasured confounding. The improvement is conditional on the usefulness of the additional source. The central contribution is a way to gain from observational predictions while protecting the generalization procedure against a poor observational study.
icml-2024-prediction-powered-generalizat.tldr: Observational prediction models can improve the generalization of trial effects to a target population while preserving robustness to poor observational data.

paragraphs: Feature attributions explain a model's prediction by assigning importance to its input features. Different attribution techniques can disagree, and a single method can produce unstable explanations. This paper asks whether combining several explanations can systematically improve their quality, making the choice of combination a problem to optimize.

The authors derive optimal convex combinations of attributions from different methods or variations of a method. In a convex combination, the weights are nonnegative and sum to one. The optimization targets desired explanation criteria, such as robustness or faithfulness to the model's behavior, and provides provable improvements for those criteria.

Experiments across multiple model architectures and popular attribution techniques show that the combination strategy consistently outperforms the individual methods and existing baselines considered. The contribution is an optimization-based way to aggregate explanations with both theoretical and empirical support. Its guarantees concern the selected quality criteria, so the improvement should be understood in terms of what the combination is designed to measure and preserve.
icml-2024-provably-better-explanations-w.tldr: Optimizing convex combinations of feature attributions yields provable improvements in selected explanation criteria and strong experimental results.

paragraphs: This paper studies how reusing training batches changes what two-layer neural networks can learn. The targets are multi-index functions, whose relevant structure lies in a target subspace. The authors compare multi-pass gradient descent with single-pass training and continuous-time gradient flow, showing that these training choices can lead to substantially different learnability conclusions.

With finite step sizes, multi-pass gradient descent can overcome limitations characterized by the information and leap exponents of the target function. Reusing batches allows the network to develop overlap with the target subspace after just two time steps, including for functions that do not satisfy the staircase property. This early overlap is distinct from completing the learning task.

The authors characterize a broad class of functions that can be learned efficiently in finite time. Their proofs use Dynamical Mean-Field Theory, and they derive a closed-form description of how low-dimensional weight projections evolve. Numerical experiments illustrate the theory. The contribution shows why batch reuse and discrete update sizes matter when interpreting theoretical limits on neural-network learning.
icml-2024-the-benefits-of-reusing-batche.tldr: Reusing batches with finite-step gradient descent lets two-layer networks overcome learnability barriers associated with single-pass training and gradient flow.

paragraphs: Transformers and state-space models are often presented as different approaches to sequence modeling. This paper develops a theoretical connection between state-space models and variants of attention. The connection is built through decompositions of semiseparable matrices, providing a shared mathematical framework for examining these model families.

The authors call this framework state space duality. Its value extends beyond describing a relationship: it guides the design of Mamba-2, a new architecture whose central layer refines Mamba's selective state-space model. The framework therefore links structural analysis of sequence models to a concrete change in how a model's core computation is organized.

The refined core layer is reported to be two to eight times faster, while Mamba-2 remains competitive with Transformers on language modeling. That speed claim applies to the core layer described in the abstract, rather than establishing the same gain for every complete training or inference workload. The contribution demonstrates how theoretical connections between model families can lead to more efficient architectures.
icml-2024-transformers-are-ssms-generali.tldr: State space duality connects SSMs with attention variants and leads to Mamba-2, whose refined core layer is reported to be two to eight times faster.

paragraphs: Prioritizing training examples with large losses or gradients can reduce the number of updates a model needs. However, computing those priorities may cost enough to erase the time savings. This paper studies a cheaper alternative: selecting examples greedily according to approximate losses instead of evaluating their exact losses.

For smooth convex losses, the authors show that this strategy can reach a constant-factor approximation to the minimum average loss in fewer iterations than random selection. They also quantify how the quality of the loss approximation affects the result. Their practical method, SIFT, obtains approximate losses by exiting early and using representations from an intermediate network layer.

Experiments train a 110-million-parameter, 12-layer BERT base model and show savings in both training hours and backpropagation steps without an optimized implementation. In one reported comparison, reaching 64% validation accuracy takes about 43 hours with a first-layer exit, versus about 57 hours for vanilla training. The empirical results demonstrate that cheaper selection can translate update savings into actual runtime savings.
icml-2024-understanding-the-training-spe.tldr: SIFT uses early-exit loss estimates to select training examples, reducing selection overhead and demonstrating faster BERT training.

paragraphs: Schrödinger bridge methods optimize transportation plans in diffusion models, but estimating their forward score functions is intractable. Training consequently relies on costly simulated trajectories. This paper introduces Variational Schrödinger Diffusion Models to improve scalability while retaining efficient transport, using variational inference to linearize the forward score functions.

The model uses a multivariate forward diffusion and adaptively optimizes the resulting variational scores. This construction restores simulation-free training for the backward scores. The authors use stochastic approximation to prove convergence of the variational scores and show convergence of adaptively generated samples based on the optimal variational scores.

In simulated examples, the method efficiently generates anisotropic shapes and produces straighter sample trajectories than single-variate diffusion. Experiments on real-world data support scalability, with competitive unconditional generation on CIFAR10 and conditional generation for time-series modeling. The method also removes the warm-up initializations required by Schrödinger bridge methods. Together, these results connect a tractable approximation of the forward scores with theoretical convergence and practical generative performance.
icml-2024-variational-schrodinger-diffus.tldr: Variational Schrödinger Diffusion Models approximate forward scores to enable simulation-free backward-score training while retaining efficient transport and convergence guarantees.
